C005.subject: GDP per capita
C005.object: material living standards in industrialized economies than median household income
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita material living standards in industrialized economies than median household income]

[PATH:empirical] Luxembourg Income Study (LIS) Database: Cross-national panel data on median household income and GDP per capita for OECD countries, post-WWII — Directly tests the comparative predictive power of GDP per capita vs. median household income on material living standard indicators (e.g., consumption, housing quality, health outcomes) via longitudinal regression analysis.

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index and related reports: Composite well-being metrics (e.g., housing, income, jobs, health) for member countries — Provides multi-dimensional measures of material living standards against which the two proxies can be correlated, allowing for variance decomposition to determine which proxy better captures non-income aspects of material well-being.

[PATH:literature] Review of income distribution and welfare economics literature (e.g., Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission report, Piketty's work on inequality) — Synthesizes theoretical arguments and prior empirical findings on why median income may better reflect typical household consumption capacity and economic security, while GDP per capita is skewed by top-end growth and non-household income.

C006.subject: GDP
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP inequality and non-market goods]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data on income inequality (e.g., World Inequality Database) and GDP per capita growth for OECD countries from 1980 onward — Directly tests whether GDP growth correlates with measures of inequality (e.g., Gini coefficient) over time in industrialized economies, providing evidence for or against GDP's failure to capture distributional changes.

[PATH:empirical] National accounts and satellite accounts for non-market goods (e.g., household production, environmental services) in industrialized economies since 1980 — Quantifies the divergence between GDP and broader welfare measures that include non-market goods, allowing assessment of how much GDP underestimates or misrepresents economic well-being in the specified domain.

[PATH:literature] Literature review of critiques and defenses of GDP as a welfare metric (e.g., Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission report, 2009) — Synthesizes theoretical arguments and empirical findings on GDP's limitations regarding inequality and non-market goods, providing a scholarly basis to evaluate the hypothesis's plausibility and identify gaps for further research.

C007.subject: GDP
C007.object: human wellbeing than the Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI)
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP human wellbeing than the Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI)]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative longitudinal studies of GPI vs. GDP per capita and subjective well-being indicators (e.g., life satisfaction surveys) in OECD countries from 1970 onward. — Directly tests whether GPI correlates more strongly with reported well-being than GDP, controlling for environmental degradation and inequality, which is central to the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Theoretical and empirical analyses of the 'Easterlin Paradox' and the threshold effect of GDP on well-being, contrasted with GPI's inclusion of non-market costs (e.g., resource depletion, income inequality). — Provides a conceptual framework and existing data to assess whether GPI captures well-being dimensions that GDP misses, especially in post-1970s developed economies.

C008.subject: GDP
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP human wellbeing]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index dataset — Provides cross-country comparisons of GDP per capita against multidimensional well-being metrics (health, education, life satisfaction), enabling direct test of GDP's explanatory power.

[PATH:literature] Easterlin Paradox literature review (e.g., Easterlin, 1974; updated studies) — Seminal and ongoing research showing that beyond a threshold, GDP growth does not correlate with increased subjective well-being, challenging the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Human Development Index (HDI) time-series analysis — HDI combines GDP with education and life expectancy; analyzing divergence between GDP and HDI trends over time can reveal cases where GDP is a weak indicator of well-being.

scope.domain: economic prosperity and quality of life

qualifier.geographic: global, with notable exceptions in developed nations

C011.subject: GDP supplemented by inequality and health metrics
C011.object: human wellbeing only in nations with high institutional trust
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP supplemented by inequality and health metrics human wellbeing only in nations with high institutional trust]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative analysis of OECD well-being indices (e.g., OECD Better Life Index) against GDP+inequality+health composites, stratified by institutional trust levels (e.g., World Values Survey trust measures) — Directly tests whether the composite's correlation with subjective well-being or other validated well-being measures is significantly higher in high-trust nations (Nordics, Germany, Netherlands) than in lower-trust OECD countries, post-2000.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal study of well-being outcomes (e.g., life satisfaction, mental health) in Nordic countries during economic shocks or policy changes, using GDP+inequality+health as predictor — If institutional trust is the key moderator, the composite should track well-being changes closely in these high-trust contexts, but fail in comparable low-trust OECD nations (e.g., Southern or Eastern Europe) during similar shocks.

[PATH:literature] Theoretical review of institutional trust as a moderator in well-being measurement frameworks (e.g., Sen's capabilities approach, Easterlin paradox literature) — Establishes the theoretical basis for why high trust might enable GDP+inequality+health to capture well-being (e.g., trust ensures public goods translate to individual welfare), and identifies conditions under which the proxy would fail, guiding empirical tests.

qualifier.geographic: OECD nations with high institutional trust (e.g., Nordic countries, Germany, Netherlands)
